title: Perfect Paper Passwords
subtitle: A free one-time password system on a wallet card
description: With Southern California's wildfires darkening the sky, Steve reviews Sony's second-generation eBook Reader, anticipates Amazon's Kindle, and shares a SpinRite story that helped a first date. Then he finishes his roaming authentication series by revealing Perfect Paper Passwords: a printed card of never-repeating four-character passcodes from a 64-character alphabet, generated by AES from a secret 384-bit key, with free code that others have already built into compatible tools, including a login module for Macs and SSH.

beats.t: This is Security Now! with Steve Gibson, Episode 115, for October 25, 2007: Perfect Paper Passwords.
Steve, with all the fires in the Southland, are you okay down there in Irvine?

Thanks, Leo. Today we'll talk about my eBook readers, a SpinRite story, and then the main topic: the second half of "Roman authentication", my free one-time password system called Perfect Paper Passwords.
The good news is I'm really close to the water, so I can jump in if I need to.
Not much reassurance for Malibu.
They're not near me, but I've been wondering about Elaine.

Coming back from refilling my Starbucks thermos, I saw our mail carrier wearing a white surgical mask. Sunday felt like the end of the world, so dark in the middle of the day. Even today the rising sun was a dark red ball from all the smoke.

I'd heard half a million people evacuated. Now it's apparently more than 800,000, and another 15,000 National Guard are coming to protect evacuated areas from looting. One fire was arson. Others were accidental sparks, from construction workers or a blowtorch, that the winds drove out of control.
Our best wishes to all our listeners in Southern California. Stay safe.
It's so sad to see fires coming up behind beautiful new housing complexes.
Nature reminds us who's in charge.
First, the news from the show's main topic. The long-awaited second half of "Roman authentication" is my solution for really bulletproof roaming authentication for my employees.

It's been up and public but not really announced, and it's caught on. Companies have written that they'll use it. Two open-source projects have published compatible implementations, and with a Pluggable Authentication Module, a PAM, you can now log in remotely to Macs with what I call Perfect Paper Passwords, PPP.
Go back to Episode 113 for the problem.
I'll recap the problem later. But first, a tech aside on Sony's second-generation eBook Reader. I heard you mention it. I bought mine the second day it was out, having read it had an improved screen.
It really does. My show notes have a side-by-side photo of the first generation, the PRS-500, and the new PRS-505. The blacks are as black, but the whites are whiter, improving contrast.
They say they sped up the page change. What they've done twists your eyeballs in their sockets.
I never liked the page change. Since it's an electrostatic screen, it has to refresh everything, like shaking an Etch A Sketch, with a flicker and flash. I lost my 500, so I can't compare.
Now it almost seems to suck the centers out of the letters, leaving outlines, then they twitter and invert. It's bizarre. I'm thinking of filming page changes.
In slow motion. I time my page turns just before the end of a sentence, since there's a pause. Sometimes I miss the last few words.
I did that too. Also, Peter F. Hamilton's Night's Dawn trilogy is available, a monster. To call it a tome doesn't do it justice. But it's a 19-megabyte download with all three books in one file.
It completely choked the Reader. I thought it had locked up. It took maybe two hours to come back, probably paginating. It's 7,536 pages in medium font. I'll read a few pages to experience it.

So it still has a first-generation feel. And in two weeks sitting off, it completely drained its battery. When I turned it on to check that page count, it said "Battery Low." Something is running inside and burning power. There should be a real off switch that disconnects the battery so it can sit six months.
On the bright side, it charges over USB and no longer comes with a special charger.
Or the stand. It's a full USB drive, so you can copy PDFs and text files to it without Sony's equivalent of iTunes.
I do that on my Mac, since there's no Sony CONNECT for Mac.
And it now has an SD card slot, instead of only Sony's proprietary format.
It comes with about 192 megabytes. Do you still listen to music on it?
I tried it once on the first one. Battery life when reading is what I like. And it recharged much faster than usual after the warning, so maybe it just needed a little hit of power.
Now you can jump to a specific page.

They moved the buttons from the bottom to the side, next to the numbered menu items, which makes sense. The old bottom buttons jumped you to a percentage, and I hit them by mistake all the time. Left on, the buttons on its face would get pushed, and I'd find the book in some lost zone.
Now you can dial page 365 and go there. Before, you could only jump by tens of percent, then painfully step. It has a ways to go, but as a reader it's nice.

chapters.title: Amazon's Kindle, and the iPhone as a Reader

beats.t: Staying with eBook readers, Amazon's Kindle is apparently days away. No big stretch for a major bookseller. They bought Mobipocket, I think, the first eBook source I used in my Palm days. Or Mobi-something.
What's interesting is that it has a built-in cellular modem on Sprint's EVDO network.
Do you need a Sprint account?

My guess is Amazon covers the downloads in some deal with Sprint. Technically it has a Sprint number, but it's only for books. For someone like my mom, who won't dock a reader to her Mac, you'd search and buy books right on the reader, and they'd magically appear.

beats.title: The Kindle
beats.t: Amazon launched the Kindle on November 19, 2007, at $399, with free "Whispernet" downloads over Sprint's network. Amazon had bought Mobipocket in 2005.
I'll get one too. But the 505 is close enough that I'm comfortable. I want paper white with black text, but it's close.
It's enough better that I'm no longer annoyed.

I wish text scaling were infinitely variable. Some books only offer small and medium, which I find hard to read. A slider would help people with low vision. I'm too embarrassed to buy large-type books, but this can grow with my failing eyesight.
On TWiT, Jerry Pournelle said the iPhone is close to being the eBook reader.
Repurposing something you already carry, for when you're stuck in line or at an airport.
And I can read much smaller type on it.
Contrast has a huge amount to do with it. As contrast drops, you need a larger font. Under bright light, I can read the Sony's small font.
With Apple's third-party apps coming, I bet an eBook reader will be one of the first.

And whatever the iPhone gets, the iPod touch gets. That's my sweet spot, if I could get my WPA key into it. Many listeners managed to enter GRC-style passwords by breaking them into four-character chunks. It took them seven tries, or 20 minutes. That's wrong. I want copy and paste.
The new BlackBerry has WiFi, copy and paste, a real keyboard, and doesn't hide the key while you type.
I'm a Treo user, so I like physical buttons. I wish the iPod touch had Bluetooth so I could use a real keyboard.
Now a SpinRite story. In my quest for interesting SpinRite stories, I'd want to call this one "SpinRite Got Me Laid."
Let's say "Made My Love Life Better."

Mike in Tucson, Arizona met a woman online, and they chatted many times before meeting. Just before, her son's laptop stopped booting, and she asked for help. So he bought SpinRite for their first date the next night.

He didn't think the date went that well, but she trusted him to take the laptop home. SpinRite fixed it, and the next day he proudly brought it back. She was so thrilled that two months later they're still dating and having a wonderful time.
It's good for your love life, ladies and gentlemen.

Now to our main topic: the second half of roaming authentication. I call it "Roman" authentication because of the Roman chair at the gym, a torture device where you hinge at the waist down to the floor and back up. Backwards sit-ups. Recap the problem.

I wanted Sue or Greg, away from home with a laptop, to reach GRC's highly privileged back-end pages: to issue refunds, look up lost serial numbers and purchase information, and email people the ability to redownload SpinRite. Everything she can do from her authorized home IP, from any IP.

At home, if her laptop lacks an authorization cookie, GRC asks whether to authorize it for roaming. She'd say yes for her laptop, and even her desktop, since her cable modem's DHCP address might change.

At Starbucks, GRC sees a request for a privileged page carrying that permanent cookie, which is only sent over SSL, so it can't be snooped. That proves the laptop was once at her authenticated IP: something she has.
She also enters a secret, unchanging passphrase: something she knows. But a keystroke monitor could record it and replay it.
So I wanted another factor that defeats even someone with perfect information: a camera, recorded keystrokes, recorded mouse clicks.
Even a keystroke logger would be thwarted.

I tried puzzles, with secret rules like summing digits and sorting letters in reverse. But I couldn't find one that someone seeing challenges and answers couldn't reverse-engineer. Saying "this is really hard, no one will get it" would be cheating. I can't allow that.

So it had to be something they carry, separate from the computer, since laptops get stolen all the time. Tokens like PayPal's, VeriSign's and RSA's need a back-end service, and VeriSign never followed through on showing me theirs. I didn't want to depend on a third party. So: something printed.
The answer is something printed. It'd be in Sue's purse or Greg's wallet, or mine. Next time I see you in Vancouver, Leo, I'll show you.

We know a good cipher, keyed with a secret and fed a counter, produces random-looking but deterministic data. That's how GRC's new Perfect Passwords page works, after analysis showed RSA's generator had less entropy than it could.
My first idea: print that random junk on an 8.5 by 11 page. Pick any random spot and type five or six characters in any direction: up, down, left, right or diagonally.

The server, knowing the key, recreates the page in memory, finds instances of my first character, checks the eight neighbors for my second to get a direction, and marches along to see if everything matches.

But we couldn't be sure we'd never enter the same sequence twice. Humans are repetitive. Something draws the eye to a certain spot. And even overlapping substrings are dangerous. Start one character over, and five of six characters repeat. With perfect information, an attacker would just test every possible sixth character, a simple brute-force attack.
The server could give coordinates and a direction instead, but the reuse problem remains.
I concluded there's no safe way to allow any reuse of data on the page, even overlapping substrings.
Because that would make it easier to guess.
It opens the system to brute-force attacks. So the user must never be asked for the same string twice.

chapters.title: Not the First One-Time Password System

beats.t: So people don't get confused, I know I haven't invented one-time passwords. FreeBSD has OPIE.
Opie?
One-time Passwords In Everything. It strings together six short words, typically four characters or fewer, drawn from a dictionary of 2,048. I've also seen commercial systems I rejected.
OPIE reuses content.
One hopes not the same set of words. But some commercial grids could lead you to type a substring of something you'd typed before. That's just not acceptable.
Next, the design of the codes: short, with a 64-character alphabet. So the design became columns and rows of separate codes. My first was 8.5 by 11, columns A through P by 50 lines. A ton of them.
I wanted codes as short as possible. Not like those insane Windows XP license keys, five groups of five, with high chances of typos. An older friend found those keys might as well have been DRM.
Short but secure means a larger character set. All those tokens use six digits, 000000 to 999999, exactly a million combinations, ten to the sixth.
A power of two is easier. Hex gives four bits per character, 32 characters give five, and 64 give six.

So I designed a case-sensitive 64-character alphabet: uppercase A to Z, lowercase a to z, and a dozen more. But many typefaces make lowercase L and the numeral 1, or uppercase O and zero, easy to confuse. So I eliminated anything visually confusing. No uppercase O or zero, even though the system could guess, because the doubt alone would create anxiety.
The 1 and lowercase L has always bugged me.

As I removed those, I needed more characters. The digits 2 through 9 are very distinct. Then I added special characters like the exclamation point, at sign and pound sign, but avoided the dollar sign, which international keyboards might lack. Every character is visually clear.
So each passcode is only four characters, like uppercase X, uppercase M, uppercase E, and 8. Four characters at six bits is 24 bits: 2 to the 24th, about 16.77 million possibilities.
Why not eight bits per character?
That needs 256 distinct characters, and there aren't that many distinctive printable ones.
So guessing a passcode is less than one in 16.77 million, versus one in a million for the PayPal, VeriSign or RSA tokens. 16.7 times more secure, Leo. And they look like little crypto things.
Easier than ten digits, too.
They're not easy to remember, since they're not words. They're easy to transcribe from your card into the screen. That's the point.

Now for the crypto inside. It's running in a demo mode at GRC.com/ppp, which forces an SSL connection. You enter a passphrase, only for the demo, because a passphrase isn't secure. The only known possible attack on this system is a weak passphrase, so no real implementation uses one.
So they generate a random key?

Even better. I used the strongest Rijndael AES, with a 256-bit key, plus another 128 bits. A counter starting at zero is added to that 128-bit value, which I call part of the "sequence key." That goes into Rijndael keyed with the other 256 bits, and out comes very high-quality pseudorandom 128 bits.

Those are taken in 24-bit chunks, each converted into a four-character "passcode," printed on a "passcard." Since 24 doesn't divide 128 evenly, you get five and a third passcodes per block. The leftover byte combines with the first two bytes of the next block for the sixth passcode.
It's all documented on the site with diagrams, well enough that two independent implementations have been written from it.

From day one I provided the code: a Windows DLL of about 16K with the entire crypto system. Give it an empty buffer, the sequence key, and say "give me so many passcodes starting here," and it does the crypto.

The whole thing is driven by a 384-bit master key. That's something like 10 to the 38th possible sequences. When you create an account, the server randomly generates your secret 384-bit sequence key, which sets your passcode sequence for all time.

beats.title: How many keys?
beats.t: 2 to the 384th is about 10 to the 115th. Ten to the 38th is roughly 2 to the 128th, the size of the counter offset alone. Either way, far too many to brute-force.
The finished product is a wallet card. That first 8.5 by 11 sheet, 16 columns by 50 lines, 800 codes, would last about three years. Ridiculous. Convenience trumped longevity.

So I designed a credit-card-size passcard. The site prints three, close together. Cut them out individually, or cut all three as a strip and fold two in, so it's back to credit-card size with three cards.
So it's a one-time pad. You use each code once and cross it out.
That's the key. Each card has columns A through G and 10 lines, 70 codes. Creating an account resets your position to zero, since passcodes are zero-based, with a secret random sequence key.
To authenticate, I give my username and passphrase, something I know, so someone who found the card in my wallet and Xeroxed it couldn't use it alone. You still need multiple factors.
Bruce Schneier believes it makes much more sense to carry something like this than to memorize a weak password.
People are already very good at protecting physical things, like paper in their wallets.

Slip it behind a credit card. But guard against someone copying it from your coat on a hanger. It's like someone pressing your PayPal token's button, reading the number and running to log in. Your login information must remain private.

The server knows where you are in the sequence. Use the first five, and it knows you're on the sixth. My implementation says, "Please type in passcode 1E on card 1." Prompting reduces no security, since it will never ask for that code again. I cross them off with a pen, which makes the next easy to find.
And if I were prompted for one further along than I expected, I'd know someone might be guessing passcodes behind my back.
Since the system only moves forward, if you think a card is compromised, or it's tattered, faded or ink-bled, just say advance me to the next card. Everything before is obsoleted.
It's a clean, elegant one-time password system with short, cool, spy-looking codes, like capital G, lowercase g, 2, lowercase v.
Now, the free code and compatible tools. There's an open-source implementation in C. My code is all assembly. The DLL is 17K, and 4K of that is an Authenticode signature.

It includes the full Rijndael cipher and SHA-384 in assembly. SHA-384 turns passphrases into 384-bit keys. The DLL can also generate random master keys from machine-specific, highly volatile information, like the number of processor clock cycles since its last hardware reset.
A newsgroup member wrote a fully compatible implementation. Given the same 384-bit key, it generates exactly the same passcode sequence as my reference implementation.
I love that people are taking it up.
Companies say they'll protect their databases with it. It handles any number of users, and passcodes go forever. Tired of being on card 492? Generate a new random master key and restart at card one.
And there's the PAM, a Pluggable Authentication Module, a standard Mac OS X supports. One person is using it to log into his Mac remotely.
Leopard comes out tomorrow with Back to My Mac, for reaching your Macs through .Mac. This could add secure login on top.
How does PAM know your passcodes?
I don't know anything about PAM, Leo. I just know he implemented it. We link to it.
The PPP pages have full documentation and a sample for printing cards. There's also an 11K EXE that exercises the DLL from the command line, so PHP or Perl sites can just shell out to it.

I don't want people saying "Gibson thinks he invented something amazing, and it's just one-time passwords." Yes. But it has cool aspects, strong crypto and neat, easy features. It secures our roaming access and will be part of a forthcoming GRC product's authentication.

chapters.title: No Key Ever Leaves the Server

beats.t: One more point about the key. Unlike a one-time pad, where you make two copies and physically deliver one, this is algorithmic.

Driven by a 384-bit key that can't be brute-forced. The only weakness would be a weak passphrase, hashed through SHA-384 to make a key, which is why real implementations generate the key at random. It only surfaces as passcodes, and there's no way to reverse-engineer those back to it.
But don't you need a handoff of that initial key?
No. The user never gets the key. After authenticating, they request passcards on their browser over SSL, print them, and carry them.
Over a secure channel, after being authenticated.

And in my implementation, a roaming laptop can't receive passcards. You print them at home. Crossing off codes shows when you're nearing the end. Fold all three cards and you have 210 passcodes, about a year's worth. It's web-friendly. Nobody mails you cards.
I'd love to use this with SSH for my web servers. It's always the same passphrase.
That's exactly what the guy who posted on GRC is doing. After his username and password, SSH prompts for his PPP passcode.
I use hotel networks a lot, so that extra bit would be nice.
And it's fun. You feel like a spy: ooh, I've got to type in :ZEY.
Laminate it? No, you have to cross them off.

Just print more when they get worn. And about your PayPal token being at home when you need it at work: a physical token's advantage is you'd know if it were stolen. But you can print two copies of your passcards and keep one locked at the office. Though who doesn't have their wallet?
That's why I like my bank texting my cell phone, which I always have.
The download even includes the HTML and CSS templates my site uses. I've done all the work. It's easy to print these cards, and they work.
You're getting perilously close to open source, dude.
We need strong authentication, and I hope the demo encourages people to adopt it.

beats.title: PPP later
beats.t: Steve later revised the system, and GRC still documents it. Today most services use authenticator apps, built on the 2011 TOTP standard, which compute a time-based six-digit code from a shared secret.

quiz.q: Why did Steve rule out letting users pick strings anywhere on a random grid?
options: People might repeat or overlap earlier strings, enabling brute force
quiz.explain: No part of a code must ever be reused.

quiz.q: Why does each PPP passcode use a 64-character alphabet?
options: Each character carries six bits, so four characters give about 16.77 million possibilities
It makes codes easy to memorize
quiz.explain: Tokens' six digits give only a million.

quiz.q: Why were characters like uppercase O, zero, 1 and lowercase L left out?
options: They're easily confused with each other in many typefaces

quiz.q: What drives the PPP passcode sequence?
options: A secret 384-bit key feeding a counter into AES
quiz.explain: The server generates it at random.

quiz.q: What's the only known attack on Perfect Paper Passwords?
options: Brute-forcing a weak passphrase used to create the key
quiz.explain: Real implementations use random keys instead.

quiz.q: Why do you still need a password along with the passcard?
options: So someone who copies your card can't log in with it alone
quiz.explain: It's multifactor: something you have and something you know.
